claims.claim: Henry Bessemer patented the Bessemer steelmaking process in 1856.
claims.episode_span: Henry Bessemer watched the same molten pig iron that had already been reduced from ore and wondered what further chemistry was strictly required to turn it into usable steel.
claims.supporting_quote: The modern process is named after its inventor, the Englishman Henry Bessemer , who took out a patent on the process in 1856.

claims.claim: Blowing air through molten pig iron oxidizes the impurities — silicon, manganese, and carbon — which escape as gas or form slag.
claims.episode_span: He asked what atoms needed to be removed from pig iron—chiefly excess carbon, silicon, and manganese—and whether the oxidation reaction could supply its own heat once started.
claims.supporting_quote: Blowing air through the molten pig iron introduces oxygen into the melt. This oxidizes impurities such as silicon , manganese , and carbon . These oxides either escape as gas or form a solid slag .

claims.claim: The oxidation of the excess carbon raises the temperature of the iron mass and keeps it molten, so no external fuel is needed during the blow.
claims.episode_span: Because the oxidation of silicon and carbon released far more heat than was required to keep the bath liquid, external fuel could be eliminated after the initial melt.
claims.supporting_quote: Oxidation of the excess carbon also raises the temperature of the iron mass and keeps it molten.

claims.claim: The Bessemer blow converted a charge of iron to steel in 10 to 20 minutes, where the prior methods took at least a full day of heating, stirring and reheating.
claims.episode_span: a charge of several tons of molten pig iron — later converters took eight to thirty tons, typically about fifteen —
claims.supporting_quote: Using the Bessemer process, it took between 10 and 20 minutes to convert three to five tons of iron into steel – it would previously take at least a full day of heating, stirring and reheating to achieve this.

claims.claim: The phosphorus limitation was solved by Sidney Gilchrist Thomas's basic process, which lined the converter with dolomite or limestone instead of clay.
claims.episode_span: that limitation was later corrected by lining the vessel with basic dolomite and adding lime, an adjustment that extended the same air-blowing principle to high-phosphorus iron without changing the core physics
claims.supporting_quote: Thomas's invention consisted of using dolomite or limestone linings for the Bessemer converter rather than clay, and it became known as the 'basic' Bessemer rather than the 'acid' Bessemer process.

claims.claim: Steel output expanded enormously after the process took hold: US output went from around 157,000 tons per year before the mid-1870s to 26 million tons annually by 1910.
claims.episode_span: while output grew by orders of magnitude
claims.supporting_quote: Prior to the opening of Carnegie's Thomson Works, steel output in the United States totaled around 157,000 tons per year. By 1910, American companies were producing 26 million tons of steel annually.

claims.claim: Bessemer announced the process in an August 1856 paper to the British Association titled 'On the Manufacture of Iron and Steel without Fuel' — the conversion needs no external fuel once the pig iron is molten.
claims.episode_span: releasing enough heat to keep the metal liquid without extra fuel
claims.supporting_quote: Bessemer felt confident enough to deliver his famous paper, 'On the Manufacture of Iron and Steel without Fuel', before the British Association for the Advancement of Science meeting at Cheltenham on 11 August 1856.

claims.episode_span: received a blast that oxidized the impurities in ten to twenty minutes
claims.supporting_quote: The Bessemer process was so fast (10-20 minutes for a heat) that it allowed little time for chemical analysis or adjustment of the alloying elements in the steel.

claims.claim: Early Bessemer converters produced steel for about £7 a ton against an initial price of around £40 a ton — a severalfold collapse in the price of bulk steel.
claims.episode_span: cut the price of bulk steel severalfold — from roughly £40 to £6–7 per long ton
claims.supporting_quote: The earliest Bessemer converters produced steel for £7 a ton, although they priced it initially at around £40 a ton.

claims.claim: The phosphorus problem was solved (1879, Sidney Gilchrist Thomas) with a basic refractory lining of dolomite/limestone/magnesite in which lime binds the phosphorus as phosphate of lime.
claims.episode_span: later corrected by lining the vessel with basic dolomite and adding lime
claims.source_title: Henry Bessemer – Man of Steel - The Chemical Engineer
claims.supporting_quote: That problem was eventually solved in 1879 by Sidney Gilchrist Thomas, who introduced a refractory lining to the converter. Depending on the quality of raw iron being smelted, the refractory lining can either consist of clay (known as the acid Bessemer process, and used for non-phosphoric iron) or dolomite, limestone or magnesite. In this so-called basic Bessemer, the lime reacts with the phosphorus to form phosphate of lime, which can be removed and used as an agricultural fertiliser.
